sections.label: ss. 51, 422
sections.citation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, ss. 51, 422

provenance.changeNote: Commencement 2004-03-29 restored from the previously verified guide (verified commencement). currentAsOf records only the review of the current wording; amendments after commencement must be checked against the point-in-time text for older meetings.

content.summary: A BC company files its annual report within two calendar months after each recognition anniversary, reporting information current at that anniversary. Missing reports do not automatically move the deadline to next year. Two consecutive years of default can trigger the registrar’s notice-based dissolution process.
content.tooltip: A BC company files its annual report within two calendar months after each recognition anniversary, reporting information current at that anniversary. Missing reports do not automatically move the deadline to next year. Two consecutive years of default can trigger the registrar’s notice-based dissolution process.
content.caveat: Dissolution requires statutory notice/opportunity to remedy and a registrar entry. An AGM, financial waiver or planned filing is not evidence an annual report was filed.
content.displayCitation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, ss. 51, 422

sections.label: ss. 42–44
sections.citation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, ss. 42–44

provenance.changeNote: Commencement 2004-03-29 restored from the previously verified guide (verified commencement). currentAsOf records only the review of the current wording; amendments after commencement must be checked against the point-in-time text for older meetings.

content.summary: Keep the statutory corporate records, including governing articles and predecessors, incorporation agreement, certificates and orders, director and securities records, shareholder and board proceedings, received consents/resignations/dissents, disclosures, financial statements and auditor representations, and conditional subtype reports. Deposit required records promptly.
content.tooltip: Keep the statutory corporate records, including governing articles and predecessors, incorporation agreement, certificates and orders, director and securities records, shareholder and board proceedings, received consents/resignations/dissents, disclosures, financial statements and auditor representations, and conditional subtype reports. Deposit required records promptly.
content.caveat: Each category is conditional on the underlying record or event existing. Section 42(1)(b) is repealed; retain the notice of articles as a governing registry record and to satisfy s. 48(2), without attributing it to that repealed paragraph.
content.displayCitation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, ss. 42–44

sections.label: s. 182
sections.citation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, s. 182

provenance.changeNote: Commencement 2004-03-29 restored from the previously verified guide (verified commencement). currentAsOf records only the review of the current wording; amendments after commencement must be checked against the point-in-time text for older meetings.

content.summary: The first AGM is due within 18 months of recognition. Thereafter an AGM is required in every calendar year and no later than 15 months after the preceding annual reference date. All AGM voting shareholders may use the statutory unanimous defer, annual-business consent or waiver routes with the applicable annual reference date.
content.tooltip: The first AGM is due within 18 months of recognition. Thereafter an AGM is required in every calendar year and no later than 15 months after the preceding annual reference date. All AGM voting shareholders may use the statutory unanimous defer, annual-business consent or waiver routes with the applicable annual reference date.
content.caveat: An extension or written alternative must be evidenced and legally applicable; a planned meeting does not reset the clock. Annual business and registry reporting remain separate.
content.displayCitation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, s. 182

sections.label: s. 1 (ordinary, special and unanimous resolution; special majority), s. 140(3)
sections.citation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, s. 1 (ordinary, special and unanimous resolution; special majority), s. 140(3)

provenance.changeNote: Commencement 2004-03-29 restored from the previously verified guide (verified commencement). currentAsOf records only the review of the current wording; amendments after commencement must be checked against the point-in-time text for older meetings.

content.summary: An ordinary meeting resolution uses a simple majority of votes cast. An ordinary written resolution is circulated to every eligible holder and needs the special majority of all entitled votes, normally at least two-thirds. A special written resolution requires all eligible general-voting shareholders. Board written resolutions default to all directors entitled to vote.
content.tooltip: An ordinary meeting resolution uses a simple majority of votes cast. An ordinary written resolution is circulated to every eligible holder and needs the special majority of all entitled votes, normally at least two-thirds. A special written resolution requires all eligible general-voting shareholders. Board written resolutions default to all directors entitled to vote.
content.caveat: Articles may set the special majority from two-thirds to three-quarters; specified legacy companies use three-quarters. Section 140(3) permits another board-consent manner authorized by the Act or articles. Class voting and transaction-specific rules also apply.
content.displayCitation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, s. 1 (ordinary, special and unanimous resolution; special majority), s. 140(3)

sections.label: ss. 140, 172
sections.citation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, ss. 140, 172

provenance.changeNote: Commencement 2004-03-29 restored from the previously verified guide (verified commencement). currentAsOf records only the review of the current wording; amendments after commencement must be checked against the point-in-time text for older meetings.

content.summary: Unless the articles provide otherwise, shareholder quorum is two entitled shareholders present personally or by proxy; where fewer entitled holders exist, all suffice. Board quorum must be resolved from the operative articles and any authorized directors’ determination.
content.tooltip: Unless the articles provide otherwise, shareholder quorum is two entitled shareholders present personally or by proxy; where fewer entitled holders exist, all suffice. Board quorum must be resolved from the operative articles and any authorized directors’ determination.
content.caveat: Table 1 articles apply only where adopted/applicable. Their shareholder percentage and board-majority defaults are not universal statutory defaults.
content.displayCitation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, ss. 140, 172

sections.label: ss. 119.1–119.11, 119.2–119.5
sections.citation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, ss. 119.1–119.11, 119.2–119.5

provenance.changeNote: Commencement of this wording is not verified. notBefore 2020-10-01 is the earliest date the governing Part could apply (Part 2.1 transparency-register provisions commenced 2020-10-01); guidance for earlier review dates carries a commencement caveat. The earlier guide's 2004-03-29 date was the Act's commencement, not this Part's.

content.summary: An in-scope private company maintains a transparency register identifying significant individuals and prescribed identity, residence, citizenship, tax-residence and control particulars. Review in the two months after each incorporation anniversary, update within 30 days of awareness and notify individuals within ten days of entering that they became or ceased to be significant.
content.tooltip: An in-scope private company maintains a transparency register identifying significant individuals and prescribed identity, residence, citizenship, tax-residence and control particulars. Review in the two months after each incorporation anniversary, update within 30 days of awareness and notify individuals within ten days of entering that they became or ceased to be significant.
content.caveat: Significance includes 25% of issued shares or general-meeting voting rights, majority-director appointment/removal control and prescribed indirect/joint control. Applicable exclusions must be checked.
content.displayCitation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, ss. 119.1–119.11, 119.2–119.5

sections.label: ss. 169–170, 219(1)
sections.citation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, ss. 169–170, 219(1)

provenance.changeNote: Commencement of this wording is not verified. notBefore 2004-03-29 is the earliest date the governing Act could apply (Business Corporations Act, SBC 2002, c. 57 came into force 2004-03-29); guidance for earlier review dates carries a commencement caveat.

content.summary: Send shareholder-meeting notice to those entitled, directors and the auditor within the prescribed minimum and no more than two calendar months before the meeting. Notice waivers/reductions and electronic-meeting instructions have specific rules.
content.tooltip: Send shareholder-meeting notice to those entitled, directors and the auditor within the prescribed minimum and no more than two calendar months before the meeting. Notice waivers/reductions and electronic-meeting instructions have specific rules.
content.caveat: The upper limit is two calendar months, not a fixed 60 days. Special business and resolutions require adequate notice content.
content.displayCitation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, ss. 169–170, 219(1)

sections.label: s. 3
sections.citation: Business Corporations Regulation, B.C. Reg. 65/2004, s. 3

content.summary: The default minimum shareholder-meeting notice is 21 days. A non-public company may specify a period of at least ten days in its articles. A public company requires at least 21 days, or the longer period its articles specify.
content.tooltip: The default minimum shareholder-meeting notice is 21 days. A non-public company may specify a period of at least ten days in its articles. A public company requires at least 21 days, or the longer period its articles specify.

sections.label: ss. 43, 46–48
sections.citation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, ss. 43, 46–48

provenance.changeNote: Commencement of this wording is not verified. notBefore 2004-03-29 is the earliest date the governing Act could apply (Business Corporations Act, SBC 2002, c. 57 came into force 2004-03-29); guidance for earlier review dates carries a commencement caveat.

content.summary: Current directors have broad inspection rights. Shareholders generally inspect shareholder-level records free; board minutes and accounting/confidential layers are not a blanket shareholder entitlement. Public companies and specified subtypes have wider public access. Copies, permitted fees and archived-record production follow separate rules.
content.tooltip: Current directors have broad inspection rights. Shareholders generally inspect shareholder-level records free; board minutes and accounting/confidential layers are not a blanket shareholder entitlement. Public companies and specified subtypes have wider public access. Copies, permitted fees and archived-record production follow separate rules.
content.caveat: The transparency register has its own restricted access regime. Section 43 permits relocation of specified records after seven years, not their destruction.
content.displayCitation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, ss. 43, 46–48

content.summary: Only directors and authorized inspecting officials receive statutory transparency-register access. Dispose of former-individual personal information in the year after the sixth anniversary of the cessation entry. Corporate and individual offence maxima can reach $100,000 and $50,000 respectively.
content.tooltip: Only directors and authorized inspecting officials receive statutory transparency-register access. Dispose of former-individual personal information in the year after the sixth anniversary of the cessation entry. Corporate and individual offence maxima can reach $100,000 and $50,000 respectively.
content.caveat: Ordinary shareholder/public record access does not extend to this register. Offence elements, defences and lawful retention duties must be considered; a maximum fine is not an automatic penalty.

sections.label: ss. 47–52
sections.citation: Business Corporations Regulation, B.C. Reg. 65/2004, ss. 47–52

provenance.changeNote: Commencement of this wording is not verified. notBefore 2026-01-12 is the earliest date the governing regulation text could apply (research records the current exclusion list as amended 2026-01-12 (BC Reg 3/2026); an older list applied before then); guidance for earlier review dates carries a commencement caveat.

content.summary: Prescribed exclusions include qualifying wholly owned subsidiaries of public issuers, certain insurance/trust and government entities, specified schools, wholly Indigenous-nation-owned companies and wholly professional-LLP-owned companies. The Regulation also defines indirect and joint control.
content.tooltip: Prescribed exclusions include qualifying wholly owned subsidiaries of public issuers, certain insurance/trust and government entities, specified schools, wholly Indigenous-nation-owned companies and wholly professional-LLP-owned companies. The Regulation also defines indirect and joint control.
content.caveat: The January 12, 2026 amendments matter. Do not use an old exemption list or apply exclusions to an entity without ownership/status evidence.

sections.label: ss. 111–112
sections.citation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, ss. 111–112

provenance.changeNote: Commencement of this wording is not verified. notBefore 2004-03-29 is the earliest date the governing Act could apply (Business Corporations Act, SBC 2002, c. 57 came into force 2004-03-29); guidance for earlier review dates carries a commencement caveat.

content.summary: Maintain the central securities register with issued and transferred shares, holders and addresses, classes/series, numbers and transaction dates/particulars. Replicate branch-register particulars promptly. The central register must remain available for statutory inspection in BC.
content.tooltip: Maintain the central securities register with issued and transferred shares, holders and addresses, classes/series, numbers and transaction dates/particulars. Replicate branch-register particulars promptly. The central register must remain available for statutory inspection in BC.
content.caveat: The Act permits specified alternative physical locations with records-office information and inspection arrangements; it does not impose a universal numeric 15-day entry rule.

sections.label: ss. 257, 259, 263–265
sections.citation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, ss. 257, 259, 263–265

provenance.changeNote: Commencement of this wording is not verified. notBefore 2004-03-29 is the earliest date the governing Act could apply (Business Corporations Act, SBC 2002, c. 57 came into force 2004-03-29); guidance for earlier review dates carries a commencement caveat.

content.summary: Articles/notice alterations follow the Act’s specified resolution, then the articles’ applicable resolution, then the special-resolution default. A notice-of-articles or special-rights alteration requires the prescribed filing and takes effect at the applicable registry time. Other article changes generally take effect when the alteration resolution is deposited at the records office.
content.tooltip: Articles/notice alterations follow the Act’s specified resolution, then the articles’ applicable resolution, then the special-resolution default. A notice-of-articles or special-rights alteration requires the prescribed filing and takes effect at the applicable registry time. Other article changes generally take effect when the alteration resolution is deposited at the records office.
content.caveat: Changing the special majority itself requires a special resolution. Class rights, names, future-effective dates and restricted provisions require their own checks; passing a resolution alone may not make an amendment effective.
content.displayCitation: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, ss. 257, 259, 263–265
